On two previous occasions this year I have dealt with the question the hon. member for Hamilton West has just raised, and I do not know that I can add anything more to it.
I know my hon. friend has read the statements I gave in answer to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, but so that there shall be no doubt about the situation, may I say this-the confusion arises, of course, because of the existence of the Old Age Pensions Act at a time when the Old Age Security Act and the Old Age Assistance Act and the Blind Persons Act are the law of the land. I think it desirable, so that there may be no confusion about this matter, to make a short statement that might be read in conjunction with what I have already said in direct answer to the kind of question raised by the hon. member a few moments ago. It should be clear that no recoveries are made from the estates of persons seventy years and over who receive benefits under the Old Age Security Act; the act does not permit it. Second, no recoveries are made from estates of persons 65 to 69 years of age who receive benefits under the Old Age Assistance Act; the act does not permit it. Third, no recoveries are made from estates of persons 21 to 69 years of age who receive benefits under the Blind Persons Act; again the act does not permit it. Fourth, no recoveries are made from the estates of persons now living and in receipt of benefits under old age security who formerly were beneficiaries under the Old Age Pensions Act. It is considered that to all intents and purposes the right to claim against the estates of these persons lapsed on January 1, 1952, when they were transferred from old age pensions to old age security. This means that the only instances in which claims are being maintained against the estates of deceased pensioners relate to instances where the pensioner was on old age pensions in 1951 or earlier when the Old Age Pensions Act was fully operative and before our new legislation came into effect. In all cases, such pensioners must have died before January 1, 1952, otherwise of course no claim would have been laid.
Claims were laid against certain estates by the provinces in 1951 or earlier but the lawyers handling the estates in some of these instances, or the executors or relatives or other interested parties, so we have been advised by the provinces, have been stalling or hesitating for one purpose or another and otherwise delaying settlement of these claims in the hope that the Old Age Pensions Act would be repealed and the claim abandoned.


Some of these cases have been pending now for over two years.
This statement I think will clear the situation in so far as the Old Age Security Act, the Old Age Assistance Act, and the Blind Persons Act are concerned. With regard to the Old Age Pensions Act, that matter is one that depends for action on the instance of the provinces. We have been in touch with the provinces, and four of them, that have a number of these cases outstanding, have not given us yet their consent or their agreement to repeal of the Old Age Pensions Act. I suspect that they wish to clear up some of these matters. In respect to some of these matters, I am sure that if my hon. friend were administering the act in the provinces- I say this because I have nothing to do with this phase of the matter-she might agree that in a particular instance there was justification for present provincial policy but there can be no question about the situation under the new federal legislation.

Of course I understand there is no question about the two new acts, and really that is what has given rise to much of the confusion. My question had to do with the Old Age Pensions Act and the answer had to do with the Old Age Security Act, which are two entirely different things.
The minister has said that he has not received the sanction of the provinces. I do not think that is true either of Manitoba or of Ontario from the information I have at hand. I find in the statement of March 17, 1953, that the minister did inform the Manitoba government that the federal government was not insisting on the provincial governments collecting the overpayments, nor did it advise them not to make such collections.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: My hon. friend is now discussing overpayments. She is not dealing with recovery from estates. There is a difference.

Yes, I realize that, and that particular point was on overpayments. But in the matter of recovery from estates, did I understand the minister to say that where a person was a pensioner under the Old Age Pensions Act and qualified under the means test provisions of that act, and received that pension, and transferred to the provisions of the Old Age Security Act, and such person subsequently died leaving an estate in excess of $2,000, no claim could be made against that estate for the portion of the pension received while he was still under the Old Age Pensions Act?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
We have no power to deal with the provinces. The provinces have their

own legislation, and administer that portion of the act. As I said when I spoke in answer to the hon. member before, we cannot interfere with them. The provinces, within their sphere, are sovereign bodies. We have no authority to tell them what they shall do. So far as we are concerned, there is no doubt about that.
Does the minister say he does not wish the provinces to collect from these estates under the Old Age Pensions Act?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I have already said we wrote to all the provinces and asked them what their views were, because the hon. member will recall they were paying a portion under the Old Age Pensions Act. The benefits the old age pensioners received came not only from us but from them. The situation now is different under the Old Age Security Act. I have no authority, nor has parliament, nor has this government any authority to tell the provinces what they must do in respect of matters which are their own concern.

Some of them at least have said that the 25 per cent, which would be their share of any recoveries from estates, does not cover their cost of administration. There is no secret about the fact that at least some of the provinces want to have this repealed. If there are provinces which do not want it repealed, and of which the minister knows, will he say that he will take no steps because such provinces have ignored the provisions of the Old Age Pensions Act?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: We do not take steps against any province.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Are we not discussing a matter which was fully debated not long ago in the house?
No.
The minister said he had written to all the provinces for their opinions in the matter. Is he in a position to put on record the answers received from them?

I would not want to do that without having first consulted the provinces. I did lay before the house the situation with respect to Manitoba, after I had received consent pursuant to a question by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Winnipeg North Centre.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I would be prepared to do that with respect to the other provinces; but first I would have to have their consent.
Supply-Health and Welfare

I should like to be clear in my mind concerning one question connected with the matter we have been discussing. An elderly lady came to see me not long ago, stating she had been a recipient under the Old Age Pensions Act, and had been receiving the pension for four or five years before the old act was superseded by the universal Old Age Security Act. A certificate was registered against her property. Now she comes under the Old Age Security Act. This point arises:	Can she sell
the property with that certificate registered against it? I called the provincial office first, and they seemed somewhat vague about the situation. Then I called the dominion office and they were just as vague. It may be that I did not speak to the right person, or to the person who knew most about it. I am not suggesting that the officials in either case were at fault, because if I did I would be unfair.
On the other hand the question arose as to whether or not this lady could sell that property, or whether the new legislation actually vacated that situation.
The new legislation could not touch that title at all. When my hon. friend refers to a certificate I suppose he is referring to liens?
Yes.

Liens were levied against estates in some provinces. In Ontario I think that practice was abandoned in 1952. But wherever there was a lien, that was initiated not at our instance or pursuant to our act, but pursuant to the act of the provinces. That was the case in the province in which both my hon. friend and I reside. But liens such as that were not the result of legislation passed by us, or anything we could do in connection with it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Oh, yes, it was.

I think the minister is going a little far afield. I believe if the officials of the Ontario government were here they would say that the dominion has a supervising hand over all this, and makes sure that these collections are made.

I can only say that my hon. friend is a lawyer, just as I am, and if he will look up the act he will see that there would be no authority for the federal government to require that. That is entirely dependent upon provincial decision, and in no way as a result of any suggestion on our part, or according to any legal authority which we could exercise.
Supply-Health and Welfare

I can understand the minister's point, that under the dominion act there would not be any right to interfere to that extent in property and civil rights. But on the other hand, as I understand it, your general regulations have to be carried out by the provincial government; and for that reason, of course, this question would arise.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: May I help my hon. friend out?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: What we did require in the regulations under the Old Age Pensions Act was that they should recover. But that is quite a different matter. The provinces did not all have liens. If a particular province used the machinery of liens, that was the decision made by it-not at our suggestion, or as a result of any authority we have. We did require, naturally, that there should be recovery. But the method of recovery was to be decided on by them.

Will the minister answer this -I do not know whether it is within his jurisdiction or not-but are those certificates still outstanding in respect of all the titles where they were filed before the universal Old Age Security Act came in?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: No; it was 1952 in Ontario. 1 am not sure about the other provinces. But in Ontario they were abandoned in 1952 by a special act of the legislature of Ontario.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: A moment ago I felt I would have to try to straighten out the record between these two lawyers. In the meantime, the Minister of National Health and Welfare has at least laid the basis for straightening it out.
The court of appeal.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Let us keep it perfectly clear that, as the hon. member for Peel says, the filing of liens is a provincial matter. It comes under property and civil rights. The federal government could not instruct and never did instruct the provinces to file liens. But the federal government legislation, under the former Old Age Pensions Act, did require that the provinces agree that they would make recoveries.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Certainly.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
And most of the provinces- I think all but British Columbia-found that the only way they could give effect to that requirement was by filing liens. It seems to me the Minister of National Health and Welfare is playing on words a bit when he says that those liens were not in any way filed at the instance of the federal government.


I think they were filed at the instance of that part of the federal legislation which required the provinces to agree to make recoveries.
However, I am not concerned about pursuing that phase of the argument, because for the most part it is now water under the bridge. In most provinces the liens have been cancelled, even in those provinces where recoveries from estates are still being effected. Nevertheless in most of the provinces acts of the legislatures have been passed cancelling the liens. From here on the provinces that are seeking to collect the money they feel they have to collect, or think they have to collect, are doing so as ordinary creditors, rather than from the preferred position of having liens against estates.
I do not wish to enter into this in detail, but there was one point I wanted to make. I confess it has been said twice already; but to my mind it is of considerable importance and should be underlined. I refer to something good that has come out of this discussion. As the minister has made clear, two questions are being discussed here this afternoon. The first has to do with recoveries from living pensioners of alleged overpayments and the other has to do with the collecting from estates of deceased pensioners.
With respect to the first question, that of collecting from living pensioners now on old age security and who were formerly on the old age pension, this now seems to be completely ended. I am glad to see the minister nod his head. Manitoba quit the practice not long ago as a result of something we need not repeat now. I think that ends that.
Apparently the other matter of collecting from estates has not yet been ended, and it is that point which the hon. member for Hamilton West has raised. But to get back to the good point that has come out of this discussion, I know there are people in Manitoba who are wondering, even after that province quit collecting alleged overpayments, what would happen if they were to die and leave estates. It is good to have the word of the minister that no claims can be filed against the estates of those who die later than January 1, 1952.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: So far as we are concerned they need have no concern whatsoever.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The minister says, "so far as we are concerned they need have no concern whatsoever". Can he not also state that that is the position taken by all the provinces, that they will not file claims against estates of pensioners who might happen to die and leave estates?
I could not guarantee that; I cannot speak for the provinces. I do not think they will, but I would not want my words to be interpreted as expressing the policy they will follow.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The minister made a definite statement a while ago that no claims would be filed against the estates of pensioners now living and drawing old age security pensions in respect of any portion of the old age pension that may have been drawn prior to January 1, 1952.
Supply-Health and Welfare

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: As far as the federal government is concerned, that is the case.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is progress and we hope more will yet be made.

speechtext:

Before the minister gets off on another track I should like to bring up one more item, because I do not think we are through with this discussion of recoveries from estates. The minister will recall that a week or two ago I spoke to him about a case. He took the correspondence and was going to let me have an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I think I can shorten things by giving the answer now.
I do not know that I want an answer now unless it is favourable.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I have done the only thing I could do. As I told my hon. friend, we have examined the situation and the matter is not one that rests with the federal government; it rests with the province of Alberta. I have written to the appropriate minister in Alberta, as I said I would, making the representations which were made to me and in respect to which I have no authority to dispose of the matter.

I would not want to interfere with the process through which this case is going, but I cannot understand the minister's explanation in respect to the matter being the entire responsibility of the province of Alberta. The correspondence I had with the province of Alberta was to the effect that they could not write off their claim against this small estate until the Old Age Pensions Act was repealed. They said they could not do it because the act was still on the statute books, and until the government chose to repeal it they were unable to release their lien.
I could not understand that because a year or two before I had a similar case. This 68108-320i
was before the Old Age Security Act came into operation. They had a lien on an estate valued at only $1,500. I searched through the records of the old age security committee and discovered that the amount recovered from estates was almost infinitesimal. I pointed out to the authorities in Alberta that recoveries from estates were progressively being reduced until the total for the previous year amounted to approximately $5,000. I pointed out to them that the estate involved was only $1,500 and that only $5,000' had been collected by way of liens. I argued that there must be larger estates in the same position and asked them to release their claim. They did that, and the woman who was the beneficiary collected.
In this instance the estate is similar, but I cannot get the provincial government to release its claim because they say this government will not permit them to do it until the Old Age Pensions Act is repealed. That is something I cannot understand. I may be mixed up, and I think the more we get into this the more we are likely to be mixed up. Do I understand that if an old age pensioner died on December 31, 1951 the province could if it chose release its claim against the estate?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That is right.
But if the pensioner died the next day, January 1, 1952, the province would have no right to release their lien on that estate.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That is not right.

Whether the pensioner died before December 31, 1951 or since January 1, 1952, if the provinces want to do so they can

Supply-Health and Welfare release all claim on their portion of the estate. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I cannot say any more than I have said on the matter. We have gone over it so often. I know the case to which my hon. friend has referred very well, because he showed me the correspondence and I agreed to assist him in any way I could. The estate there is under $2,000. If I remember rightly it is $1,700. There is no difficulty. I will not say that the province of Alberta will release it, but they have the authority to give a release in an estate under $2,000. If my hon. friend will just leave this with me I think he will find that we will achieve the same success through my intervention with the province of Alberta as we did in the other case.

I thank the minister and I hope he is right. I wanted to settle the question of whether or not the provinces were bound because the Old Age Pensions Act is still on the books. The minister evidently says they are not, and that if they wish to release their liens they can.

I am sorry, but I am still not satisfied. I do not think the minister has said yet that the province has a right to relinquish its claims upon the estates of these people against whom they had claims under the Old Age Pensions Act. I know it is perfectly true that the federal government does not instigate these actions or make any claims against these estates, but is it not true that the provinces are still responsible to the federal government for collection from these estates? It seems to me that it is in line with what I said previously about the 25 per cent which is coming to the provinces not being sufficient even to pay the cost of administration. It is the old, old story. The coat and the pants do all the work and the vest gets all the gravy.

Two hon. members have mentioned the allowance for the blind. Last night the matter was brought up by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, and this afternoon the hon. member for St. John's West again raised the question.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: We covered that last night. I thought we had an agreement last night that we had covered it.

I did not hear any agreement reached about the blind allowance being covered, and actually it comes under this particular vote. The minister replied on both occasions that nothing could be done about removing the means test from the blind allowance without first reaching agreement with the provinces. He made no further comment whatever about the suggestion that the means test should be removed. I think he should go a little further, because I do not believe

that answer has anything whatever to do with the proposal put forward by the Canadian national institute for the blind and by the Canadian council of the blind.
As I understand it, the situation with respect to pensions and security is that before the Old Age Security Act came into effect, old age pensions and blind pensions were on the basis of the dominion paying 75 per cent and the provinces paying 25 per cent. When the Old Age Security Act came into effect the dominion took over payment of everything both for the sighted and the blind 70 years of age or over. In other words, the provinces are now paying nothing towards old age security.
On the other hand, the old age allowance for people between 65 and 69 is paid on the basis of 50 per cent by the dominion and 50 per cent by the province, subject to a means test. But the allowance for the blind under 70 is still paid on a basis of 75 per cent by the dominion and 25 per cent by the province. If I am wrong, perhaps the minister will correct me.
That is right.

What has been asked is that the blind allowance be put on the same basis as old age security, in other words that the dominion make the whole payment so the provinces will not come into the picture at all.

My hon. friend asks me a question. The C.N.I.B. have not asked that. They have asked that the means test be abolished, but they have not asked us to shoulder the responsibility because the provinces make a contribution. They have asked that the means test be abolished, which involves action by us and by the provinces.

I do not believe the minister is correct in his understanding of what is being requested. So far as I am concerned, I believe the proper course to follow would be for the dominion to pay the allowance in full rather than getting 25 per cent from the provinces, and I also believe that it should be paid without a means test. I suggest that for these reasons. When the pension was made available for the blind the thought was that they were being treated in exactly the same way as Canadians who were getting the old age pension. Right down through the picture the Canadian people generally thought that the blind were being put in the same position as old age pensioners. I think it is reasonable that they should be. Because of their great handicap they should be treated in the same way as former old age pensioners who are now the recipients of old age securtiy. I am quite

confident that a large majority of the members of the house feel exactly the same way. Members from all parties believe that the blind should be put on the same basis as recipients of old age security.
The reason this measure for the blind was first adopted was in order to help them in some small way to get on an even basis with the sighted. It was meant as a compensation for their disability and to give them a chance to get an even start with sighted Canadians in the race of life. The trouble with a means test is that it has the effect of discouraging the blind from trying to carry on and earn their own living. That is particularly true in the case of people who have become blind after becoming adults. I have been associated with work for the blind for many years. No doubt other hon. members have as well, and when these people face this terrible disaster of blindness it is frightfully difficult for them to make the decision that they will go ahead and earn their own living in spite of their handicap.
The very fact that there is a means test and that if they do get out and make a living they may not be able to obtain the help arising from the allowance is enough to discourage some of the blind. I do urge that the means test should be abolished and that the dominion government should take full responsibility for payment in exactly the same way as is done under the Old Age Security Act. The two associations that presented the brief to the minister, which I believe was dated January 14, 1953, are thoroughly responsible associations, as he knows.
No one knows that better than I.
They have a splendid record of statesmanlike leadership of the blind over many decades.
I am sure my hon. friend would agree that I know that even better than he does.

They have summed up this request in a very reasonable way, and I should like to read from their comment on the suggestion that the means test be abolished. I am quoting from their brief of January 14, 1953:
The loss of sight for any human being is a tragic occurrence and brings in its train, fear, frustration and insecurity.
Since over SO per cent of the blind lose their sight in adult life, it is obvious that each of these individuals has actually been deprived of a priceless possession. When we lose something that we have grown accustomed to and have become dependent upon, the implications are obvious. We recognize the desire and applaud the obvious intent of the government of Canada to assist the blind through the allowances provided under the Blind
Supply-Health and Welfare Persons Act. However, when these allowances are made conditional, subject to the means test, notice is served on a newly-blinded person, already suffering from a sense of desperation and insecurity, that he must accept the allowance in comparative idleness or be willing to take a chance of loss of the allowance by reason of earnings, however insecure. This choice too often reacts as a negation of ambition and effort. We who are interested in the fullest exercise of all talents by the blind and stimulation to the most normal range of activities, including work and productivity, deplore this effect. We respectfully draw attention to the fact that in our competitive form of society, we encourage individual ambition and effort to achieve a normal standard of living.
That sums up the situation very clearly, I think. Also, the aim of the leaders of the blind is very well shown by the attitude of Colonel Eddie Baker who has been a key man in the work for the blind ever since he lost his sight in the first war. I remember walking down the street in Vancouver with Eddie one afternoon. He is not the type who holds your arm or hangs back. He walks right ahead as though he had his sight. I said to him: "Eddie, you are going to hit a telephone pole if you walk ahead like that." He does not admit that he has any handicap, and he said "I walk like other people, and if I hit a telephone pole it is going to be too bad for that pole." That is the attitude Colonel Baker has taken right down through the years, and I think the parliament of Canada could do nothing less than to remove this means test on the blind of Canada.
I realize that it cannot be done at the present session, but I would hope that it would be one of the first moves of the next parliament of Canada, no matter what party may form the government.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
We of this group would like to urge that the minister and the government give more serious consideration than they have yet given to the representations made by the Canadian national institute for the blind and the Canadian council of the blind. The minister has indicated that he knows what their requests are. He has indicated his knowledge of these people and his interest in them. Well, I hope he will show that interest by more active consideration of this whole question.
I think I know, as a result of having been on the old age security committee three years ago, something of the thinking of the department with regard to this question. I believe there is a feeling on the part of the officials that at least the government has done nothing in the change that has been made to worsen the position of the blind. They are still getting the same amount of pension they were getting before. From age 21 and up they are still getting that amount, and there has been a slight improvement over what the

Supply-Health and Welfare situation was prior to January 1, 1952, in that if they are over 70 although these people do not get the blindness allowance they get the old age security pension free of the means test, as does everyone else.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that what is overlooked is the fact that under the former legislation, before January 1, 1952, we did give to our blind persons in receipt of pensions a very slight advantage over sighted persons on the old age pension.
In common with the member for Van-couver-Quadra I would like to have the attention of those to whom I am speaking.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I can listen to you, too; time is going on.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: But the official to whom you are listening is an important one.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I find you both interesting.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, prior to January 1, 1952, we did give to the blind a slight advantage over sighted persons. It was not an advantage in dollars as far as the pension was concerned, but there was an advantage in that the means test provision was less strict. That meant that those over 70 who were on the blind pension could, if they were able, earn a little more outside income than was the case with the ordinary old age pensioner. As far as those from 21 to 69 were concerned they had a slight advantage, in that they not only received the blind pension but they had a means test which was a little less strict than the old age pension means test.
Now that slight advantage has been taken away, at least in so far as the blind person over 70 is concerned. He is no different from his counterpart who is sighted, although between the ages of 21 and 69 there is the slight difference as far as means test is concerned. Even in respect of burnt-out pensioners under the War Veterans Allowance Act-and we are complaining about the means test there-we make it possible for the veteran who is over 70 to draw $20 of the burnt-out pension and, as well, the full old age security pension; but we deny that advantage in the operation of the blindness allowance to a person over 70 who goes on old age security.
I am not going to take time to develop it further. Indeed what I am arguing for now is a lot less than I think should be done, a lot less than is suggested in the brief of the two blind organizations. I would urge the government and the officials dealing with this matter to face up to the fact that in our view, and in the view of many members of the house, we have not dealt squarely with
[Mr. Knowles.l

our blind people. We owe them much more, as an act of ordinary decency, than we have given them thus far.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I shall just take a moment. I am sure my hon. friends would agree with the observations made by the blind people themselves when I saw them a short time ago. They regard the treatment we have given them as not deserving of the description that we have not given them square treatment. No person in the association would say that. They have always said the opposite. They are very grateful; they know of the sympathy of this government; and they know that the problem is one which involves both the federal and the provincial governments.
It is all very well to say that the federal government can do it all. That is easy to say; but one forgets that, as a result of the passage of the Old Age Security Act, we have relieved the provinces of a total annual commitment of over $18 million in respect of old age pensions, including pensions for the blind. In asking the provinces to bear their share we are not only living up to good social standards but we are also asking something which, at the present time under the constitution, is necessary.
I just want to remind the house that in 1937 from this side of the house we introduced blind pensions. It was from this side of the house that the age was reduced to 21, and it was also from this side of the house in 1951 that the residence requirement was reduced from 20 to 10 years. It was also from this side of the house that the income ceilings were raised in 1944, 1947, 1949 and 1951; so that we on this side of the house have a deep and genuine interest in this program as have, I know, those hon. members who have spoken and as indeed have all hon. members of this House of Commons. I can say that I am sure this matter will be explored and that the federal government will be most anxious to ascertain the results of representations that are being made in other quarters. This matter is receiving our active and enthusiastic interest.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Will the minister just take a minute to clear up what I think is some confusion with regard to figures. I asked him a question last night to which he gave the answer as reported at page 5032 of Hansard:
The result would be that only about 5,000 blind pensioners would be involved.
I thought at the time that he had said 4,000, and I repeated it as 4,000. But Hansard reported him as saying 5,000.
I gave the correct figure.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Then I asked some questions as to what that figure involved. A few minutes ago this afternoon the minister gave us figures indicating that there are 8,332 persons in receipt of the blind pension. Can he straighten out those figures?
Seventy-five per cent of those are already getting the full pension; I mean 7,500.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Seventy-five per cent?
7,500 of those are already getting full pension.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Seventy-five per cent would be about 6,000. That means that there are about 2,000 under 69 who are not getting the full pension and 3,000 over 70?
7,500 of the 8,300 are getting the full pension.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Seventy-five per cent?
I say, for the third time, that 7,500 of the 8,300 are getting the full pension.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: So the figure of 5,000 is made up of the other 800 under age 69 and-
That is right.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: And the balance are blind persons over 70 who are on old age security rather than on the blindness allowance?
I will give that information to my hon. friend. Surely we do not need to go into those details at this late stage.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I think it would take about two sentences for the minister to put the matter straight on the record.

All right. More than 6,000 blind persons 70 years of age or more are presently getting their old age security pension free of the means test. That would be over 30 per cent of the total blind in Canada. The proposal to abolish the means test would not be of any help to those.
More than 8,300 of the 12,000 blind between the ages of 21 and 69 are already receiving blindness allowance. Ninety per cent or more of these are receiving the full amount of $40 per month. The average amount paid to all 8,332 blindness allowance recipients in March, 1953, was $39.57. The abolition of the means test from the blindness allowance would therefore benefit the 8,300 present recipients of blindness allowance by only 43 cents a month on the average. In actual fact, it would not benefit 7,500 of the 8,300 at all. The remaining 800 would benefit partially, of course.

I shall detain the committee for only a moment. I am interested in this matter of civil defence, and I am wondering

whether the minister under whose department this item comes has given any thought to what might be a wider scope of national defence by doing something to prevent saboteurs from stopping industry, wrecking trains and so forth.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Permit me to indicate that the estimates of the Department of Justice will be up shortly, and in so far as sabotage is concerned the work of civil defence is carried on by the officers of that department along with others in the Department of National Defence. It is not a matter that specifically arises out of this vote.

I could wait, but what I have to say I shall say only once anyway. Let me put it this way. Has the minister given any thought to the opportunity for poisonous chemicals to be used in sabotage? The other day the minister was asked by the hon. member for Peace River a very important question in respect to the fluorination of water. The minister may carry my observations to the Minister of Justice if he wants to. If the enemy should desire to do so, what measures would there be to prevent them from placing men in strategic places in Canada where they could poison the waters of certain cities overnight in the same way as they would apply fluorination, only in extra quantities using some other chemical, so that by breakfast time next morning the city would be a graveyard?

My hon. friend can be assured that this matter is being followed very closely by the officers of the departments I have mentioned as well as by our own industrial hygiene division and by the defence research board.

In connection with this item, can the minister give us a general statement as to the progress that is being made? This matter of civil defence has been under his supervision now for a period of about three years. The importance of it is evident to all. In view of the number of volunteers across Canada who are participating in this activity, public attention by the House of Commons is proper in the circumstances. Perhaps the minister would favour us with a general statement as to progress. We have in his annual report noticed the progress made up to March 31, 1952, but a year has elapsed 68108-321
Supply-Health and Welfare since that date and there are quite a number of items of considerable importance that we might discuss.

I can only say, as I said last year, that the government looks on this difficult matter of civil defence as a matter which should engage government efforts on all levels, municipal, provincial and federal.
Our civil defence plan is modelled on that of the United Kingdom, where emphasis is laid upon the important part, the all-important part, that must be taken by local bodies. A civil defence organization is incapable of successful action unless on the local level there is the greatest of interest, co-operation and contribution. We have given expression to that principle in a financial way, more generously on a comparative basis than is done in the United Kingdom whose plan we have followed.
We have felt that our responsibility at the centre is to train the people who carry on this work at the local and provincial levels. And at our school here, under the chief direction of the co-ordinator of civil defence, General Worthington, we have trained over 3,000 individuals who have gone out to the provinces and the municipalities and in turn have taken charge of civil defence direction on these levels. We pay the expenses of the individuals who come from afar to Ottawa, provide their maintenance and of course provide completely for the upkeep of the school.
We provide certain types of equipment, all based on agreements we have had with the provinces as to the course of action that should be followed. We provide the sirens, and under the matching arrangement we have with the provinces we provide for the installation by assuming half of the cost thereof. We provide the equipment for civil defence workers; we take practically exclusive responsibility for the educational material, represented by our budget of some $300,000 odd, composed of film strips, films, radio talks, pamphlets and the like. In addition we supply such things as fire pumpers.
We have engaged in programs of standardization of hose couplings with at least two of the provinces, Alberta and Ontario. We have regarded as our exclusive responsibility the stockpiling of medical supplies, perhaps one of the most important things that we at the centre can do. We bear the full responsibility of that. It is a program that when com-
5076	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare pleted will entail an expenditure of about some $9 million. But it does not represent an actual expenditure, an actual loss, because most of the supplies purchased are capable of redemption for other purposes. We have not gone into the business of dealing with perishable drugs, but by an arrangement that we have with drug [DOT] companies we will have available the required amounts in the light of what we can now see.
We provide rescue vehicles and maintain warning systems. We have a warning system here at the centre, of course, altogether independent of the communications system of the Department of Transport and of the Department of National Defence. I think we can say that we are building our civil defence organization on responsible and sound lines. No one can ever say that a civil defence organization is adequate, and I would not want to say that ours is, nor would I want to say that any country's civil defence organization is adequate.
We have to take into account the assessment based on what we believe to be the state of international tension at the moment, and we have to govern ourselves accordingly. That is not always an easy thing to do. It would be easy to build up an organization to key pitch that would be capable of being destroyed by inactivity or non-use, and that is something that we have had to guard against just as they have been guarding against it in Great Britain. Sir John Hodsoll, who was head of civil defence in Great Britain during the war, and who is perhaps the most experienced in civil defence certainly known to us, is in continual liaison with Canada. He visits us periodically, and our officers visit him. Some of our officers take courses in his school, and there is a reciprocal arrangement in that particular.
So I can say that a civil defence organization has been built up which provides, as we now do, for the volunteer effort of some
135,000	people in the country. This represents a contribution indicating the extent to which our preparations have led us thus far, and the sincerity and determination which lies behind that effort.

Mr. Chairman, I represent a constituency which is particularly conscious of civil defence, because of certain circumstances. A number of groups there during the last two or three years have given a great deal of their time to the organization of civil


defence on a local basis, and have been most successful.	.
During the last two or three years a number of these men have come to Ottawa to attend the school. Let me inform the minister that, naturally, they all came to see me when they were here-and they were pleased to see me-and they have all told me they were pleased with the arrangements at the school, pleased with the course and with the instructors. In all cases they were the type of men well able to judge administration and organization. They were also pleased with the emphasis now being given to doing this work from a long-term viewpoint, and considering it not only as civil defence in the event of a war but as civil defence by way of organizing communities so there will be permanent organizations able to cope with disasters at all levels.
There was one point they all brought to my attention, and which I noticed the minister mentioned in his remarks. They all informed me they were anxious to see standardization of hose couplings, concerning which I understand arrangements have been made with two provinces.
We are prepared to make arrangements with all the provinces, but thus far arrangements have been made with only two.

These men were deeply interested in the subject. That was the one point on which they were all agreed, that they hoped it would not be long before there would be dominion-wide arrangements to bring about a standardization of hose couplings.
I thank the hon. member for what he has said.
With regard to the minister's statement that 135,000 people have received training in civil defence, I wonder if he could give a breakdown by provinces to indicate the progress being made.

Yes. If hon. members wish,
I could take the time to read it. However, if it is satisfactory I would be prepared, with consent, to place it on the record.

We are all anxious to complete the business of the session, but this matter of civil defence is important. The matter of hose couplings was mentioned a moment ago, and the minister said Ontario and Alberta had completed arrangements with the federal government. What has caused delay in completing arrangements elsewhere?

As my hon. friend understands, the standardization of hose couplings is a matter which would not only be valuable in civil defence or in the event of disaster, but something which would have a permanent all-time value in any community. Having that in mind, we have offered to the provinces one-third of the cost of the program in each province. Ontario now has such a program under way, and so has Alberta. We are now negotiating for the same arrangement, under which we would assume one-third of the cost, in British Columbia. No such accord yet exists in my hon. friend's province.

In common with other countries, we are experimenting with shelters. I would want to examine more closely the precise statement my hon. friend has mentioned. speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I would not for one moment suggest that the 128,000 are all at the top level of training of those who have been to the school to which the hon. member for Kootenay West referred a few moments ago. The figure of 128,000 trained personnel is perhaps misleading unless you look at it more closely. After all, the average volunteer starts off with basic training course A or something like that. The figures I have given were supplied by the provinces. I have not the percentage of actual training. Of the 128,000 civil defence workers a certain number have received training. A great number of them have taken the full curricula available and to the extent that it is possible to offer it. I have here a statement which was made by Sir John Hodsoll with reference to our organization a few months ago in which he says:
I was immensely struck with the keenness of everyone in the organization there. There is general agreement at the top as to the importance of civil defence and great interest is taken in it everywhere.
And again:
From all I saw I formed the impression that civil defence in Canada is making splendid progress. I do not know of any other jurisdiction where in so short a time such progress has been made.

I think we ought to be realistic about this. Either it is serious or it is not serious. If it is serious I think it is foolish to let it go at this point with just a few generalizations and a vague figure of 128,000 who have been trained. The minister has told us in general terms that there is co-operation with the provinces, but actually we have not the slightest idea as to the number of communities in Canada where there are people competent to take charge of the situation. Surely that is the test. Again at the risk of being tiresome may I say that I sympathize with the minister's difficulties.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
There is not a city in Canada with a population of over 50,000 which has not a civil defence director, except two.
Supply-Health and Welfare There is not a city of over 75,000 population in Canada which in our judgment has not a competent civil defence organization, with the exception of four communities. I do not think it would be in the interests of the esprit de corps we are trying to build up that I should be asked what cities those are.

I will not ask what they are. What the minister has said carries me one step further. The minister has indicated that he has to rely a good deal on provincial organizations, which is natural enough. I should like the minister to say whether he is satisfied, whether he has such co-operation from these provincial organizations that he can tell us that there is a staff in every city in Canada of any size, with the exception of the two he mentioned? Can he tell us what these organizations mean? Does it mean that there are a few people who in their hearts know what should be done? Does it mean that in city X you have a staff in every ward or in every section, and what does that staff do? Are they just cherishing the knowledge which they have? To what extent are they in touch with the ordinary citizen?
We are not going to have a day or a week or a month's notice during which they can make up for lost time. I am not trying to paint any blood-curdling picture of what is going to happen, but if this thing comes it will come in a hurry and probably without: any warning. I do not think the minister should leave us with the impression that we have a civil defence organization that is ready to step into action. If the minister tells me that I am wrong, I have respect for his opinion; but if I am not wrong then it: seems to me we should not be left with the impression that things are pretty good.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I thought I had been frank with the committee in my statement. I am certainly not going to 'say to my hon. friend or to the country that I am happy with the state of civil defence. There is no country in the world where that could be said. It is just one of those things that you cannot be happy about. What we have done has been done in the light of what we think we should provide for financially and otherwise. We can only judge in the light of those standards what we think is our immediate job.
As I said at the outset, we do not want to build up to the maximum point and needlessly raise enthusiasm that will suddenly drop, so when you really want it you are not able to get it. We are building along solid lines. For example, Vancouver has a budget of $200,000. They have people per-

Supply-Health and Welfare manently engaged. Edmonton has its underground system. They are now giving consideration to their communications centre in Winnipeg. I do not want to say that, if anything happened at this minute, the civil defence organization could take care of the kind of disaster that could conceivably happen. Is proper attention being paid to co-ordination of training between cities and surrounding municipalities so that evacuations can take place in the case of some disaster occurring in the city itself?

offering any criticism of them at all. I am simply referring to them in passing. This is a task which has not been done except perhaps in certain places. charge of civil defence would be held responsible, and he might conceive then that his role of usefulness in public life had gone. I do not doubt that for a moment.
Nevertheless, having said that, I think we do have an active system of education. Every province but one has its own public information division and public information officer. They work directly with the schools, as they feel they should, and with other bodies. I will hurriedly give a few examples of the new training manuals we have prepared. With regard to the percentage of civil defence workers in the population which is deemed desirable in a civil defence organization, the estimated requirement is 2 per cent. It may be under or over that figure, but that is the estimate given by those who should know.
