Is the minister making a statement now?
No.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to make some remarks on this general item. I do not intend to take a great deal of the time of the committee, though not because this is not a very important matter. We all know that the Department of Veterans Affairs is one of the most important departments of our governments. That is so because it has to do with the lives and hopes of some of the most patriotic citizens in this country.

Supply-Veterans Affairs The Department of Veterans Affairs dealt primarily with men of the first war; and the men of 1914 to 1918 are now old men. It has been a long time since the end of that war. The work of the department in regard to them is concerned mostly with pensions, war veterans allowances, hospitals, old soldiers' homes-provisions that need to be made for the older veterans.
The next problem of the Department of Veterans Affairs is, of course, care of veterans of the second world war. Those men who returned five or six years ago are now just getting nicely started in the life of this country. I think we can feel very proud indeed of the manner in which they are progressing in business and professional life, farming, fishing and, in fact, in all stages ctf life in this country. You might say that they are doing very well indeed in every walk of life. As a matter of fact it has been a matter of some amazement to see the manner in which the young men and young women of Canada can change from war to peace and from peace to war.
I think it will also be fair to say at this time, Mr. Chairman, that in the veterans charter and in subsequent legislation we have good legislation as far as our veterans are concerned. I think we can say that the affairs of veterans in this country are well administered. I say that keeping in mind the fact that we have at the head of the different branches of the department men who had proven themselves in wartime and who, in peacetime, have been doing a very good job as far as veterans are concerned.
By that I do not mean there are still no weaknesses in our veterans' legislation. I do not think anyone would agree with me if I made that statement. We have found throughout the years that there is nothing static about veterans' legislation. There has been change right through the piece. We have had a great many veterans affairs committees and, as all members of those committees know, we have had to provide for many changes in veterans' legislation. As our first war veterans grew older new legislation had to be brought in. When the second world war came legislation had to be prepared to look after the requirements and rehabilitation of those men. Now we have veterans of the Korean war, and again there has to be provision for the men in that conflict.
However, I think we will all agree that one of the greatest problems we have today in our veterans' legislation concerns the older men. As I said a few moments ago, the men of the second world war are settling down and 
seem to be carrying on very well indeed under the legislation we have provided. The chief criticism, I think-I know, in fact-has to do with the War Veterans Allowance Act. All members of the house are familiar with this act. It was passed back in 1930, in the days of the depression. It was passed then to assist in keeping our veterans, who were becoming aged, off the breadlines, as stated by the then minister of veterans affairs.
There have been many changes since 1930 and one of the greatest changes, of course, has been in connection with the age of the veterans. The men who in 1930 were in their forties and early fifties are now in their sixties and seventies; so, naturally, there have been many changes and there are many more men receiving benefits under the War Veterans Allowance Act today than in the early days. The changes have mostly been in the amount paid as allowance. At first it was $20 for a single veteran; later that was increased to $40 and, last year, it was increased to $50 a month for the single veteran and $90 a month for a married veteran.
There is the matter of the cost of living, the great cost of everything the veteran or anyone else has to buy. That has been the chief reason for the change of amount of monthly allowances. In 1952 the War Veterans Allowance Act was before the veterans affairs committee. At that time the committee was asked to increase the basic rate of the allowance. It was increased from $40 a month to $50 a month for single veterans and from $70 to $90 a month for married veterans. At that time the veterans' organizations appearing before the committee felt that the amount was not large enough and, as a matter of fact, the veterans' organizations presented very substantial arguments before our committee advocating that the amounts should be larger. However, those amounts were decided on.
Since that time there has been more abundant proof submitted to the government by veterans' organizations that there should be a further increase due to the high cost of living. As I have advocated many times before in the House of Commons, I think during this session of parliament there should have been a veterans affairs committee which could have considered this request of the veterans across this country for a further increase.
One of the main changes in the legislation of 1952 was the provision in section 4 for monthly employment of veterans. At that time I remember that the minister and others contended that this provision would be a

great help in giving employment to our veterans, and that it would be a great blessing for the veterans in receipt of war veterans allowance. Some months ago I had brought down in the house a return showing the number of veterans who had taken advantage of section 4 of the amended act. While I myself had not expected that there would be a great many, still I was greatly disappointed at the extremely small number who had taken advantage of this section. As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, out of approximately 30,000 men under the War Veterans Allowance Act, only 258 took advantage of section 4.
I should like to read just what the minister had to say in this connection in order to show that the department and, I think, the minister expected from this particular section far greater results than those which followed. In June, 1952, speaking before the national council of the Legion and discussing the amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act, the minister said:
To my mind the most important feature of the proposed legislation is the introduction of a new provision which will permit income earned during a temporary period to be exempted.
Then he goes on to say:
Under the present legislation the earnings of a recipient are limited by a ceiling computed on an annual basis, which has the effect of penalizing the man who is, from time to time, able to earn more than the ceiling allows. The proposed change is to stimulate personal enterprise and encourage our older workers to stay in employment, even on a temporary basis, as long as possible. It is our belief, as I am sure it is yours, that the average man is happier with a job; it gives him the feeling that he is useful, contributing something to society. For the ordinary man it is the basis of self-respect.
That was the opinion the minister had in 1952. As I pointed out just a moment ago, out of 30,000 war veterans under the War Veterans Allowance Act only 258 have taken advantage of this section. To me that indicates-as I know it must to the minister also- that the provisions of the section were extremely disappointing indeed. The result is not to be wondered at because, as I said a few moments ago, these men are of the average age of 64 or 65. They are not physically fit. Both their age and their physical condition militate against permitting them to carry on work even on a monthly basis.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to discuss further this matter of the ceiling set by the War Veterans Allowance Act. While we all feel that perhaps the basic rate should be increased, I think the chief objection which is taken by veterans and veterans' organizations all across the country, as well as by the press and by people in general, is that
Supply-Veterans Affairs the ceiling which was provided in the legislation in 1952 is too low. This matter has been discussed in the house on many occasions and it is not necessary to go into it to any great extent today. But I would remind you, Mr. Chairman, that in 1952 the ceiling on earnings, instead of being increased as far as war veterans allowance was concerned, was reduced both for the single veteran and for the married veteran until today it is only $120 a year. That is, $10 a month over and above the war veterans allowance is all that a single or a married veteran is'allowed to earn. This situation is so manifestly wrong that I expected, as I am sure most of the members of the house did, that an amendment to this act would be brought in during this session. These men under the war veterans allowance, with this ceiling, are in a strait-jacket. They can earn practically nothing except this small pittance, as I say, of $10 a month.
Besides earnings, there is also the case of the small disability pensioners. This subject has also been discussed on many occasions. [DOT] As to the pensioner whose pension is less than $50 a month, he also is entitled to war veterans allowance if he is in needy circumstances. If he receives war veterans allowance and if the ceiling remains at $720 a year, he gets practically no benefit, because the pension is deducted from his war veterans allowance. In his case a higher ceiling would help materially.
Then again there is the person with a small superannuation allowance. He is in practically the same position as that of the small pensioner. There is no encouragement for these men to provide a superannuation allowance for themselves because, with the war veterans allowance ceiling as it is, there is again a deduction from their allowance.
Again, there is the pensioner over 70 years of age. The Legion has felt-as I am sure many hon. members have-that besides the war veterans allowance these men should be allowed to receive their old age pension. We see men in other walks of life, wealthy men, who receive their $40 a month besides their superannuation allowance and whatever other provision they have made for their old age. But a veteran over 70 years of age cannot receive his old age pension and his war veterans allowance if the two are above the ceiling which I mentioned.
I think this situation also is so manifestly wrong' that some increase in the ceiling should have been made; and again I repeat that it should have been made this session.
I cannot understand why a measure to amend the act was not brought in. With respect to

Supply-Veterans Affairs war veterans allowance and the old age pension, some people will say that the war veterans allowance was given to men at 60 because they were aged by the hardships undergone in the war to the extent of an extra ten years, and it is really an old age pension. We all know that we have gotten a long way from that idea. It is really not an old age pension at all. If it were, every man who served in the first war and who today is over 60 years of age would be considered to have aged 10 years and under the Old Age Security Act a pension which is given without means test at 70 should be given to a veteran over 60 without a means test; that is, if they carried out the argument that it is an old age pension. There is also the veteran who is capable of doing a day's work occasionally. He may be a watchman. He may be engaged as janitor of a school or a church. This man is not allowed to engage in that kind of work and at the same time receive the full war veterans allowance if the two are over and above the ceiling which I mentioned.
I should like to read, from page 26 of the ' proceedings and evidence of the special committee on veterans affairs of 1952, a statement of one of the witnesses who appeared before that committee. We were discussing Bill No. 181, which had to do with war veterans allowances. In this instance they were giving an account of a woman who had written in regarding some work that she was prepared to do. Her husband was suffering from diabetes and unable to work. This is the part I want to quote:
Whilst my husband was in hospital our minister offered us a three-room house with light and water and $50 per month. I told him we could not accept the salary, but would be glad to accept the house and light free in exchange for caretaking of church property-but that we had better consult the war veterans allowance board first. We have just received the letter tonight. Believe it or not, if we take this house and light and donate our work to the church the war veterans allowance will deduct the rent value from his allowance.
This women goes on to say:
In the name of God, what kind of a system is this?
She could not understand. I do not think it is necessary for me to elaborate this matter further. The whole thing is that the ceiling on the war veterans allowance, as I said a few moments ago, has these people in a strait-jacket and something should be done and done at once to bring about an amendment to this act.
Another subject which has been giving great concern to veterans all across the country is the matter of housing. This subject has been discussed quite thoroughly in the house and it is not necessary for me to do more


than bring it to the attention of the committee at this time. In 1946, as we all know, it was considered by the Legion to be a very serious problem, and they set up a committee to investigate veterans' housing conditions all across Canada. The situation has changed very little since 1946 as far as housing is concerned. The information we received a few weeks ago in a debate on housing was that between 500,000 and 600,000 houses were needed in Canada. Last year the Legion dominion housing committee in their investigation reported that 60 per cent of those needing houses in Canada today are veterans. In their report at that time they said that this was partly due to lack of material, and also to lack of qualified workmen.
The evidence that came before us a few weeks ago in the debate showed that there was no great lack of material or of tradesmen. The trouble is that today the price of a house is far beyond the reach of the ordinary man. A man must have an income of at least $3,500 today to provide himself with a house. That is the evidence that was given before one of the committees. Very few workingmen have salaries of $3,500 or more. The other alternative is a rented house. The average rent today is somewhere around $80 a month.
A few days ago I was going through one of the cities in this country and I met a young man who had been in my training camp during the war. He went overseas afterward. He, his wife and his four children were sitting in a park. I asked him how he was making out. He said: "I am doing fairly well but I cannot get a house to live in. We have two rooms." He, his wife and his four children were living in two rooms, and he said it was an impossible way to live. What was true of this young man is true of thousands of others across this country.
I know this is not entirely the problem of the Department of Veterans Affairs; it is a problem, however, affecting veterans and I repeat, had we had a committee to study this matter of housing and other matters we might have been able to make some recommendations to the government on housing. It is a problem not only in this country but in the United States. I feel free to suggest that our veterans department could do something in this connection, because it is a matter that is receiving attention by the veterans administration in the United States. A few days ago I read in one of the United States papers an article which said:
All government-required down payments on G.I. home loans are slated to be removed within a few

days, the veterans administration has announced through its Boston office.
Under the new regulations, world war II veterans and Korean war veterans will no longer be required to make down payments on V.A.-guaranteed loans under government restrictions.
This will open a vast new field of prospective home building throughout the country, the administration believed.
There is more to the article which I will not read; I simply call it to the attention of the committee to indicate that this matter is receiving very serious attention by the veterans administration in the United States, and it is a matter serious enough to receive attention by our veterans administration in this country.
There is another matter to which I should like to call attention. I am speaking of matters that could have been discussed by a veterans committee if one had been set up. I have said time and again that we should have a permanent veterans committee. I now refer to the question of war prisoners. A few days ago the Secretary of State gave some reason why the government did not hear the representations of an organization known as the national council of prisoners of war. This national council of prisoners of war are war veterans. They are returned men who suffered over a period of years in the war camps of Germany, Italy and other places where prisoners had been taken. I am not saying that these men should receive what they ask for. I do not know. What I do contend is that they should have received more attention from the government. I also contend that if we had had a war veterans committee-
I do not like to interrupt my hon. friend, but I want to tell him that this association was received by the government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Twice.
They were received not more than ten days ago, and they made their representations.
They were received by certain members of the government.
That is what they had asked for.

They came back and asked for another conference with the government. In any event, Mr. Chairman, their petition or brief did not receive the attention it should have received. That is the point I am making. The war veterans committee would have shown them more courtesy.
Oh, no.

The committee would have made a more careful study of the brief
Supply-Veterans Affairs presented. I am not advocating that they be given what they asked for, because I do not know whether or not they are entitled to it. But I do know that I have studied the report of the advisory committee on war claims, made by Mr. Justice Ilsley. I know he recommended that the Hong Kong prisoners should receive so much a day on account of maltreatment. I know he recommended that the prisoners under the control of the storm troopers in Germany should receive so much.
These men contend that the Geneva agreement was broken, so far as they are concerned. Anyone who reads their brief will see they contend that under the terms of the Geneva agreement they are not receiving the treatment they should receive. In Mr. Justice Ilsley's report the chief reason given for granting relief to the prisoners of war who came under the storm troopers in Germany is that they did not receive the treatment they should have received under the Geneva agreement.
I am sure the suffering of these men who make application was not as great as the suffering of the men at Hong Kong; I am sure they were not treated as badly as the men who came under the SS. troops; but it is all a question of degree. And it is quite possible that a committee studying this matter would have granted them at least a portion of what they were requesting.
They are not asking the government to give them something from the national income. They are not asking for a raid on the treasury. This is not government money; it has to do with reparations obtained from Germany and Japan to the extent of about $9 million, paid in settlement of claims. It is a question whether it is to be paid to prisoners of war, such as these, or to be paid for loss of property. That is the question.
As I say, these men are not asking for any raid on the treasury. I saw an article in the Legionary not long ago which made some comment about men surrendering easily. Well, I do not think anyone can claim that Canadian soldiers have ever surrendered easily. For instance, in the Korean war, in all the time our men have been fighting in Korea, only a small handful of Canadians have surrendered. Read the history of the first war; read the history of the second war. No, I do not think we need fear that making payments to these men, if they are entitled to it-and that is something which should have been determined by a committee of the house-would encourage in any way

Supply-Veterans Affairs the surrendering of any of our troops at any time in any war.
Then there are other matters which could have been discussed this year by a committee on veterans affairs. There is, for instance, Bill 336 which makes provision for higher education for the children of deceased members of the forces. That bill was discussed in the house, and some of us expressed the view that they should be treated the same as single veterans. I believe the recommendation from the veterans committee was that they be treated in that way. Well, they are not. To put the matter in a nutshell, single veterans received $60 a month as university students while the children of deceased veterans are to receive $25 a month, over and above other payments for tuition, etc. This is something which might very well have been discussed in the committee on veterans affairs.
Then there was one section in the superannuation act, a contentious section which had to do with the soldier settlement board and the old department of soldiers civil re-establishment. The feeling was held by most members in the committee that something should have been done for these men. What excuse has been given? Why has it been recommended for study at a future session? The statement is made that there was no time to study the question now. Again I say if a veterans affairs committee had been set up it could have been studied by that committee and satisfactory provisions could have been included in the superannuation act.
There are some other matters I should like to mention, but as it is almost six o'clock I shall not speak longer at this time. My main argument is that, despite our legislation for veterans-and it is good-there are weaknesses in it. The great weakness is in connection with war veterans allowances. I know veterans all across the country have been greatly disappointed, as I have, that no provision was made this year to raise the ceiling and, if necessary, increase the basic rate of allowance.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before you call it six o'clock, there is one matter I should like to put straight, and that is with respect to representations made by the prisoners of war association. They are a national association and they did ask to be heard by the cabinet two months ago-that is, to meet a committee of the cabinet. On that occasion the organization was asked to meet with a minister of the cabinet, and the Minister of Veterans Affairs was selected. Naturally he


was sympathetic to their representations, and promised to present their case to the cabinet.
After they returned home and discussed the matter among themselves they made a second appeal to meet with a committee of the cabinet, feeling that they wanted to meet more of the cabinet than only one minister, and pointing out that they had some fresh arguments to present. That opportunity was given to them within the last two weeks; I do not remember the exact date. A representative committee of the cabinet did meet with them, discussed their problems at length and promised to refer them to the whole cabinet. It is incorrect to say that they had an unsatisfactory hearing and that they have appealed against it. They asked for a second hearing; they have had both hearings, and now await a decision.
But they were turned down, as was announced by the Secretary of State two or three weeks ago. What hearing was that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: If there was any rejection, I am not aware of it.
It was announced in the house.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
If there was a rejection, it would be between those two hearings. But within the last ten days they have had a hearing before a committee of the cabinet. That is what they asked for, and their case is in process of consideration.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, the first thing I want to say is that my experience with the senior officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs has always been most pleasant. They have not always given me what I wanted, but I must say they have been most courteous. In so far as the act permitted them to do so they have given me every co-operation and assistance. Only yesterday I visited the Veterans Land Act office, which is under Mr. Rutherford, and I must say to the minister, through you, Mr. Chairman, that the officials there are doing an excellent job in the performance of their duties.
Possibly a lot of the discussion we have had would have been unnecessary if the minister had made a statement at the opening of his estimates. We would not have had the discussion on prisoners in Hong Kong. I think we should have had a full explanation at the start. However, that is the

prerogative of the minister. I do not think anything is going to be gained by a speaker rehashing what has taken place or what has not taken place. I do not think we are going to help the veteran that way. The concern of those of us who are veterans is to endeavour to help our fellow veterans.
We did not have a veterans affairs committee during this session, but I think the first thing the minister should do at the next session is to set up a standing committee on veterans affairs. I believe every hon. member would agree to that. I know the people of Canada would agree, and I know that organizations such as the Legion think we should have it. There are several excellent veteran organizations in Canada. I am biased in favour of the Legion because they have the largest membership and I happen to be a member myself. I think they bring down excellent and reasonable briefs.
The main thing I am going to speak about tonight is the war veterans allowance. I regret exceedingly that no action has been taken this session in connection with this matter. Possibly if the distribution of these veterans had been more even across Canada there would have been some action taken this session. Fortunately or unfortunately-I believe fortunately because we are proud to have them-some 27 per cent of those in receipt of war veterans allowance reside in British Columbia. I am being a little critical when I say that perhaps other hon. members do not take the interest they should in these veterans because they probably are not familiar with their problems. Because of our climate and for other reasons many of these veterans took their discharge in British Columbia at the end of the war, and others have moved to our district since.
I agree with much of what the hon. member for Royal said, but I disagree with other things he said. I believe the ordinary layman and even medical science are beginning to realize that a veteran who had served in the front line was pre-aged by at least ten years. I am not saying that this would apply to the man who served in an administrative capacity in England or at Le Havre, but certainly the man who had the misfortune to serve in the infantry was pre-aged by at least ten years. I feel that that fact should be taken into consideration in connection with these allowances.
I cannot conceive how anyone can defend the means test in connection with war veterans allowance. As has been pointed out already, the casual earnings such as a veteran might make might just as well not be permitted at all. That is just what it amounts
Supply-Veterans Affairs to. If the recipient of a war veterans allowance earns anything he is immediately penalized. Surely it is not the desire of the people of Canada that that should be so. This could be remedied at this session by the simple stroke of a pen to wipe it out.
I do not think the amount of the war veterans allowance is large enough. We have not taken into consideration the increases in the cost of food and everything else. I think we have the finest veterans' legislation in the world, and I am prepared to defend it anywhere; but that does not necessarily say that it is good enough. As one hon. member of the opposition said about another matter, where is the money coming from? The people in my riding object to paying taxes just the same as the people in other ridings. We would prefer to have to pay no taxes at all. If we have to pay them, we want them to be as low as possible.
But I feel that every taxpayer, not only in my riding but in other ridings of British Columbia, would be willing to pay whatever taxes were necessary to see that the veterans, particularly the elderly veterans, are properly cared for. I am not advocating to the government that taxes be kept as high next year or even increased. I certainly intend to be in this seat next year in order to advise the government. Obviously our national defence expenditures will not be as high next year. That is a matter of common sense. We have built all these buildings that are necessary and unless we have actual war we will not need the same amount of money for defence purposes. Let us give some of it to the deserving veterans.
Another matter I should like to bring up in connection with war veterans allowances and in which I think the department has fallen down is the insistence on the repayment of any overpayments that have been made. Before the act was amended many veterans made something through casual employment and their allowance was still paid. They have been called upon to pay that back to the department. I do not think the Department of Veterans Affairs should follow the example of the income tax branch.
If the Department of Veterans Affairs makes a mistake and overpays a veteran, instead of trying to collect it from the veteran they should write it off in their profit and loss account as is done in all government departments as well as in private business. If you are in the farming business you write it all off to loss. To me it is absolutely unfair that these people should be called upon to repay these amounts to the department.

Supply-Veterans Affairs
I repeat that I do not think anything is to be gained by rehashing mistakes that have been made in the past. We have good legislation, but it is not good enough. I do not know if I am permitted to refer to the budget debate. I have got through almost to the end of the session without breaking any rules, and I do not want to break one now.
I told the Minister of Finance at the time I made my budget speech-I think I am entitled to refer to my own speech even if I do, not refer to his-that he was one of the finest ministers of finance we ever had in Canada, but that he had the opportunity to go down in history as a great minister of finance if he would increase the war veterans allowance. I am glad to see that he is in good humour after his trip, and in excellent physical condition. Before he goes fishing it would be a very simple matter to pass an order in council to rectify his omissions of the past so far as the war veterans allowance is concerned. I can assure him that he will have the support of everybody in the province of British Columbia.
I want to reiterate that in my opinion the first committee that should be set up at the opening of next session is a standing committee on veterans affairs. We have standing committees on agriculture and almost every other conceivable subject. We have a standing committee on printing which I think has met once in 13 years. Yet we do ourselves proud by having the names of the members of that committee printed in an official booklet. I have been honoured by being made chairman of it, and I do not think it has met since. The point I am getting at is that there is nothing for these committees to do. The committee on agriculture only sat in the last four or five days. Agriculture is a big business. Then there is that nonsensical committee that brought in a report the other night on a divorce bill that is costing the taxpayers of Canada $1,200. That committee wastes its time considering such a matter.
Surely a standing committee on veterans affairs could be appointed. I am sure no member of the house can point to anything more important than the veterans of Canada. When we stop to realize that none of us would be sitting here today if our veterans had not been willing to fight in two great wars in the past, then surely we should be able to set up a standing committee to consider veterans affairs. In the past the veterans affairs committee has been made up of members of all parties, and I do not think the members of any committee of the house that has ever met have been more imbued with a spirit of trying to work with one


another irrespective of party politics. As we saw it, we were working together on behalf of the greatest resource Canada has, its veterans and their dependents, the veterans who fought on our behalf.
I am proud of the legislation we have, and I am prepared to defend it on the platform or elsewhere. I am prepared to say it is as good as any in the world; but I still think that, although it is almost the end of the session, something should be done about the war veterans allowance. It certainly is very close to the end of the session so far as I am concerned, although I realize that the house may be able to struggle along for a day or two without my valuable services. However, even now I ask the government to rectify what I think has been a mistake during this parliament, the mistake of not providing a proper reward for war veterans allowance recipients.

Mr. Chairman, our group has arrived at an understanding that I will occupy a few minutes on the minister's estimates so the remainder of the group will not have to take up too much time. I have no hesitation in taking up a few minutes of the minister's time because of a conversation I heard in the cafeteria this morning. The question was being discussed at a nearby table as to when we might get away from here. It was said that the ministers were getting a bit jittery with their estimates, and were becoming a bit impatient. One chap at the table said there was one minister coming on tonight whom we did not have to worry about, the Minister of Veterans Affairs. He said that the minister was so interested in his department and the people for whom he is legislating that he would gladly stay for a week to listen to members who may have complaints.
That is right.

I was a bit hesitant as to whether I should say very much, but after hearing that assurance from a person who knows the minister quite well I felt the minister would be relaxed, and he looks relaxed right now. I know he is interested, and wants all the advice he can get.
Like the hon. member for Fraser Valley, who says he is going to send me Hansard next year, I too should like to take this opportunity-one never knows who will come back-to pay tribute to the many officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs and the pension commission from the chairman down, because those who administer the legislation can only go as far as the legislation permits them. I have always found that the different

sections of the department have been most expeditious and courteous in dealing with mail and supplying other information. I want the minister to know that he has an efficient department.
Turning to the legislation itself, much of it is good. However, veterans' legislation is a social program for men handicapped because of war service; and a social program, like life itself, cannot be measured in terms of days and years. There is no finality to it; it goes on and on. The minister, the department and the government may be quite proud of the veterans legislation compared with such legislation in other countries; nevertheless it is the duty of members, particularly opposition members, to try to make it better and to see that a program of social security is continued for handicapped veterans who cannot take their regular place in the scheme of things.
Every member receives many letters dealing with war veterans allowances, pensions administration and so on. Some of them are pretty critical. For example, I received one a few days ago on the question of the war veterans allowance. The writer had a bad story to tell, but I want to tell the minister how he started his letter. It will give him some idea of the thinking of people outside the house who believe that they are legitimately entitled to something under the legislation. He commenced his letter by saying: "On a hill far away sits an old rugged boss who ignores both suffering and pain." Then he went on to give the minister quite a licking, indicating that he was in a very critical frame of mind.
I think there are gaps in the legislation that should be filled. The major issue raised by Legion branches and the national organization during the last year concerned the necessity of amending the War Veterans Allowance Act. That was the major issue they posed. I think their demands are reasonable in the light of prices today, rents, food supplies, clothing and the general cost of living. The Legion asked for an increase in the war veterans allowance from $50 to $60 for a single person. I do not think that is an unreasonable demand. The minister must realize that when you go to look for a room in a city like Ottawa you find that it will cost you $40 a month just for a place to sleep. There would not be much left for food, clothing and what have you if you were getting $60 a month. It would be very skimpy; you would have to eat in Bowles' restaurant, and you would not have very many clothes. I think it is reasonable to request that the single persons' allowance should be increased to $60 a month.

They ask that for married veterans the amount be increased from $90 to $120. A married person generally has a few dependents and cannot live in one room. With rents as they are in this city, to get an apartment with a couple of rooms and a place to cook costs $80 a month, which is about the cheapest I have seen. The married veteran has not much left after that for the other amenities of life.
The second point which the Legion stresses very strongly, and it has all kinds of implications, is that we should remove the means test in war veterans allowances; and if the means test is not removed, they say we should step up the permissible earnings. At the present the ceilings are $720 for a single person and $1,200 for a married person. The Legion asks that the amounts be increased to $1,200 for single persons and $2,000 for married persons.
The means test in war veterans allowances is a handicap. It is a handicap when the veteran reaches the age of 70 and receives his old age security pension of $40 a month, because then his war veterans' allowance is decreased in that amount. Stepping up the permissible earnings in my opinion is not going to cost the government anything. It would provide an incentive for the single veteran who is able to do so to go out and take some employment to bring his income of $720 up to $1,200, and the married veteran could supplement his $1,200 and bring it up to $2,000. I think it is a point the government should consider, because it is all to the good if these people can go out and earn extra money and contribute something to the pool of wealth. You hear a lot of people in this house arguing for free enterprise. They say it creates the urge to go out and get more for yourself. If it is a good principle in general business it should be a good principle to establish in respect of war veterans allowances, especially in view of the fact that it is not going to require any more money from the treasury. I would ask the minister to consider that particular point seriously.
The next point about which the Legion is concerned is the extension of the war veterans allowances to include men who served in England in world war I. England was not designated as a theatre of war during the first war. The men who served in England then cannot receive war veterans allowances. In the last war England was considered to be a theatre of war and men who served there during the second world war are entitled to war veterans allowances. As the minister knows, many older veterans are writing in about this. They are broken down now, they have never established a disability pension,

Supply-Veterans Affairs and they cannot be employed at the present time, particularly in heavy industry. Most of my correspondence comes from that section; and those veterans think it is a pretty rank piece of discrimination when young men who served in the last war and got to England are eligible for war veterans allowance. The older veteran perhaps had considerable service in England and was kept there because of the type of service he was performing. We had records offices in England in the first war, and hundreds of personnel were stationed there by virtue of the positions they held and the qualifications they possessed. They were kept there despite their wishes. As a result they are not eligible for war veterans allowance. I think the government should have considered that point a long time ago.
The next point stressed in the Legion representation to the government concerns the removal of the residence clause for widows of imperial veterans. If the husband did not reside in Canada for the full 20 years before passing away, the widows are not entitled to war veterans allowance. There are many cases, of course, where the man passed away after being in the country only five or ten years. One can understand that cut-off. However, when the ex-imperial was within a few days, a few weeks, or a few months of being in the country 20 years when he passed on it is rather tough for the widow, who may be living in the same section of a town as the widow of a veteran who just happened to get over the line of the residence clause. The one qualifies and the other does not.
I think this is something that should be corrected. All along my opinion on the matter has been that for these older imperials there should have been some discretionary latitude given to the commission in order to take care of these borderline cases. Practically all the cases I have seen are right on the borderline and the husbands have been within a few months or a few weeks of completing the required time of residence in this country.
There is another point which I would like the minister to think about. There is discrimination as between province and province in the matter of a widow who is the recipient of war veterans allowance. The provinces that have not passed it have not done so for the reason that their provincial income does not permit the additional expenditure of money.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare knows very well, from his experience in his grants in aid that are contingent upon the province matching them dollar for dollar, that some of the provinces-four at least-have not as yet been able to take their share of what was granted because they were not able to match dollar for dollar with the federal government. The same thing applies in veterans' legislation with regard to the widow being able to receive both mothers' allowance and full war veterans' allowance.
Legislation of that kind in my opinion is designed to help people in provinces which have greater income because of their geographic position. That is true whether it is legislation on national health and welfare or veterans affairs.
I do not think that is equality in Canada as most of the members of the House of Commons want to see it. It is not Prince Edward Island's fault that it is down in the section of the country where it is. It is not Newfoundland's fault that it has not the resources

that Alberta and British Columbia have. It is not the fault of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick that they are located geographically in a section of Canada that prevents them from fully developing and marketing their resources in the central Canadian provinces. I consider that kind of legislation to be discriminatory.
If the federal government is going to have legislation designed to better the condition of widows under the war veterans allowance, I think when that legislation is established it should be made uniform and that every widow across Canada should be treated in exactly the same way. The service given by the person in the province with a low provincial income was exactly the same as the service rendered by any other soldier in the Dominion of Canada. I want the minister to think about that matter. Let us not get into the habit in this country of developing a program of social security, either for veterans or for the average citizen, designed to help the provinces that have the greatest incomes. Let us at least try to make our social security measures uniform and applicable to all citizens across the country.
There is another point I should like to make, and it is one which the minister and I have argued about and have written about to a considerable extent. I refer now to the gratuity credits.

I got in touch with the minister to find out whether those credits could be paid outside of Canada. The answer was no. It was granted by the Canadian government for the purpose of rehabilitation. She located in British Columbia. Both she and her husband found that, in order properly to set themselves up in life, there were greater opportunities in their professions in the United States; and like hundreds of other Canadians they shifted to where they could do the best for themselves.

The second case that has been brought to my attention is that of a former captain in the army. He lived in my part of the country, then went to Saskatchewan and lived there for some time. But there is the old homestead there, and when the boy visited his home he said, "This place looks as though it needs to be fixed up." He was born there. He said to his father, "Go ahead and fix it up. This is going to be my home in the future. I carried on a considerable amount of correspondence with the department as to whether in a case of that kind, the credits could not be considered as part of the boy's estate and be passed on to his next of kin as such. It was admitted by the department that at the time of his death that particular boy was contributing approximately $40 a month toward the maintenance of his parents, and that all during his period of service he did contribute to the maintenance of his parents. I do not think any law should be as firm as that. Certainly in this case, and in several others like it, there are extenuating circumstances. I realize that the lawyers who draft the legislation do so from the legal point of view, and that they make it as airtight as possible. But I think even in this case there is flexibility, and that the question of "wholly dependent" is a matter of interpretation. The fact that that boy was renovating the home in which he figured he would live in the later years of his life, and the fact that at his request the parents undertook the obligation of renovating that home at some considerable expense should, I believe, be taken into consideration.
In this particular case I think the department made a mistake. In my opinion those who interpreted that "wholly dependent" could have granted the rehabilitation credits as part of that boy's estate. I hope the minister will take a look at that case some time.
I am not blaming anybody. As I said when I started, the departmental officials can go only as far as the legislation will permit them to go. But in this particular case I think someone should take a look at it and see whether something could not be done to carry out the last wishes of that boy as expressed the last time he was home.
All this adds up to the fact that I agree with the hon. member for Fraser Valley, the hon. member for Royal and many others who over the past couple of years have said that a standing committee of the House of Commons should be set up to deal with veterans affairs.
Since 1945 the House of Commons committee on veterans affairs has not been a committee of this house on veterans affairs. It has been a committee appointed for the purpose of examining legislation, not to study and recommend but to examine legislation drafted and referred to it, which is a completely different thing. In 1940 when the committee was first set up for the purpose of opening up the old legislation and relating the new forces to it, we did not just go in and study the bills; we went in there and examined the whole question. Out of the deliberations and studies of that committee came a whole lot of the legislation that is contained in the veterans charter. But in the past few years the committee has been examining proposals that were already drafted, upon which it had not been con. suited.
The minister and the government are making a mistake. If we had a standing


committee whose job it would be to watch and follow the trend of veterans' legislation or the necessity for changes, the biggest asset that the minister and the department could have would be 25 or 30 veteran members of this house. They could sit down out of the realm of politics and make a study of what they thought was fair and reasonable, and the minister could check it from time to time. In that way he could be getting a large group of members of this house to share responsibility with him for veterans' legislation, and many times he would find the members of that committee on his side in controversial matters which arise in the house because the average member has not an opportunity to study the material. I refer to such matters as we have been discussing tonight, namely softening up the legislation that prevents departmental officials from making a reasonable decision where there are extenuating circumstances with respect to such questions as rehabilitation credits as part of the estates of persons such as those I have been talking about. There are complaints that cannot be anticipated by the average person who sits down and writes legislation.
Then with respect to the veterans allowance and all these changes that we have been talking about, instead of it just coming up at a moment's notice and all hon. members expressing individual opinions, the committee would have a chance to debate these things through and have a general understanding of them. They could consult with the Legion from time to time, and out of these discussions and deliberations would come recommendations on problems that arise in the country.
As I said when I opened my remarks, this is social legislation for the person who has become handicapped through his war service. There is no finality to it. It is going on, and we might as well realize that the best way of handling it and keeping it within reason is by having study going on all the time by men who are veterans themselves, who are members of the Legion and of the House of Commons, and who would rather work with the minister on finding a solution to these problems than have to fight with him from time to time.

I have a few matters that I should like to bring up. After listening to the assurance of the hon. member for Cape Breton South that the minister will welcome all the advice we can give him at this time, I am no longer hesitant in taking a little of the time of the committee.

We in this group would like to join with those other hon. members who have urged upon the government the setting up of a permanent standing committee on veterans affairs. At the present time we allow grievances of veterans and grievances of various organizations to pile up. Then after two or three years we set up a committee to deal with those grievances; but in the meantime a certain amount of discontent has grown and even when the committee is set up that resentment continues. We feel that if a standing committee was set up it could make a full review of the grievances of the veterans, and then there would be a better feeling among the veterans' organizations.
I would agree that the veterans' charter provided for a very fine program of veterans' legislation. I would also say that the officials of that department have done all they could to administer it fairly. I know, in so far as I am concerned, I have always felt that the officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs did give every consideration to the cases that I referred to them. By that I do not mean for one minute to say that they always did those things that I wanted them to do. But when they turned me down I did at least feel that they had gone as far as they could within the confines of the act, and that is as far as they can go.
Although the veterans' charter did provide a fine re-establishment set-up for veterans, nevertheless time has gone on, and the time has now come to review that legislation and revise some of it. Unfortunately, when the special committee on veterans affairs has been set up in recent years it has not been allowed to make a general review of veterans' legislation. Invariably it has been tied down by the terms of the reference to deal with specific items; therefore when the veterans' organizations appeared before us requesting that we do this or that, we have had to tell them that our terms of reference permitted us to deal only with specific items. I am sure the minister will agree that this has caused a certain amount of resentment on the part of veterans' organizations.
After the first war we had the department of soldiers civil re-establishment. That was considered to be a temporary department, apparently. It was thought that after a few years most of the veterans' problems would disappear, and as time went on perhaps the department would disappear also; but no one would suggest for one moment that today the Department of Veterans Affairs is a temporary department. For that reason I say we should have a permanent standing committee on veterans affairs, and not just a temporary
Supply-Veterans Affairs one set up as the government may see fit from time to time.
One of the most important pieces of veterans' legislation was the War Veterans Allowance Act. I would call the War Veterans Allowance Act the veterans' last resort. I am now referring to the disabled veteran. If a veteran is unable to obtain a pension owing to some slight technicality within the Pension Act, or if because of the fact that his disability is not attributable to war service or because his disability is of preenlistment origin the request for a pension is turned down, then he has to depend on the war veterans allowance in order to get an income. The important thing to keep in mind in regard to the War Veterans Allowance Act is that only those veterans who saw service in a theatre of actual war are entitled to get that allowance, unless of course they are in receipt of a small pension. We should keep that in mind at all times, because some people think it is something to give to any veteran who gets hard up or is unable to get a job or gets a little bit disabled. After all, any veteran who remained behind in what the soldiers called a "cushy" job is not eligible for the war veterans allowance. He must have seen service. That should always be kept in mind.
There is no doubt that some improvement was made in the act last year. We increased the amount of the allowance by $10 a month for single veterans and by $20 a month for married veterans, but we made no increase in the amount of permissive income over and above the allowance. As a matter of fact we reduced it for married veterans from $250 down to $120. That was due, of course, to the increase in the amount of the allowance. The present ceiling is altogether too low, $720 for a single veteran and $1,200 for a married veteran. It makes it almost impossible for the veteran today to have what you might call a reasonable standard of living, unless he is in a position to qualify under section 4 of the act.
While section 4 may provide quite considerable benefits for a veteran who is able to get a job for a month or two, it is of absolutely no use to the disabled veteran who is not able to work. He cannot come under section 4. Only that veteran who is fortunate enough to be able to get a good job for a short time benefits. He can go on a monthly instead of a yearly basis and, as a result of the money he earns during the month, he will not have his allowance reduced in future months. Section 4 is a good section, and I was sorry to hear that so few veterans have taken advantage of it.

But, as I said at the time we had that legislation before us, the veteran I am most worried about is the one who is unable to work, and is receiving war veterans allowance. We did very little for him last year. True, we increased the allowance by $10 a month, but we did not raise the ceiling on incomes. Therefore if a veteran happened to be fortunate enough to have a small legacy left to him, or was able to get some form of pension in addition, he was denied the full benefits because of that ceiling.
The Legion filed a brief with the federal committee last year, and I think their brief was generally quite reasonable. They asked that the ceiling be raised from $720 to $1,200 for a single man and from $1,200 to $2,000 for a married man. That is approximately the level of income we have established as the minimum a family or person should have to live on in this country. The exemption in respect of income tax is set at $2,000 for a married man and $1,000 for a single man. I presume when the Minister of Finance placed the exemption at that level he had in mind the fact that a person needed that income in order to be able to live. Therefore no taxation was placed upon individuals with income below those amounts. If that is true of the average Canadian, it must also be true of the veteran. Therefore I think the ceiling on incomes should be raised to at least the level of the exemptions for income tax purposes, in order to bring the veterans up to parity.
Then the Legion also urged an increase in the allowance from $50 to $60 for a single person and from $90 to $120 for a married person. I think that was reasonable, in the light of the heavy increase in the cost of living we have been encountering during the past few years. I am satisfied the government would not be subjected to any embarrassment from the standpoint of public opinion if they were to make these increases. They would have the full force of public opinion behind them if they were to introduce legislation of that kind.
I was interested last year in listening to a certain person in the Department of Veterans Affairs-I have now forgotten his name- make some observations on a subject in which he was interested. I believe it was described as a science and, although I am not quite sure as to the proper word, I believe the science was described as geriatrics. No doubt it has considerable merit in it. However, I have felt some concern in the matter, and in discussing it with other veterans I have heard them express concern, too. They are fearful that that science will be used for the purpose of trying to dig out the old veterans, the ones who are burnt out, in an effort to get them into some kind of employment.

I agree that in some cases that may do some veterans a lot of good. But I am afraid there are other veterans who would like to retire and take it a little easier, but who will feel that they have to go back into some form of employment so they will not be accused of taking the war veterans allowance improperly. I hope departmental officials will be careful not to put undue pressure upon veterans, in the light of this science of geriatrics. As a matter of fact, that is an unfortunate term; it sounds too much like gerrymander.
Then I would raise one other point in connection with war veterans allowances, and that is in connection with the widows of imperials. I think we made a big mistake when we refused to give war veterans allowances to the widows of imperials who have resided in this country for 20 years, but whose husbands died before they had completed 20 years' residence. I find it hard to understand the reason for this procedure.
I can understand not paying war veterans allowance to a widow until she has completed 20 years of residence; but just because her husband had the misfortune to die before he had completed his full 20 years residence in this country seems to me a very peculiar reason for denying that widow the war veterans allowance. That matter should be dealt with next year; I suppose it is too late to do it this year.
Then for a few moments I should like to discuss questions related to the Veterans Land Act, in so far as small holdings are concerned. At present the requirement is that a veteran must buy three acres of land. For a time we lifted that requirement in one section of Ontario and allowed veterans to take small holdings of half an acre. I understand the present requirement, however, is that they must have three acres of land when they build a house.
I have discussed this matter with a number of Veterans Land Act officials in western Canada, and they tell me the picture is greatly complicated. They say they would like to see the three-acre regulation reduced to half an acre, because the requirement that a veteran must buy three acres of land is greatly increasing the cost to him of acquiring a home. Three acres of land can only be had at considerable cost whereas, if the amount were reduced to half an acre, the veteran would have to buy only that much land.
I fully appreciate the original purpose. The idea was that the veteran would have three acres of land and would be able to supplement his income by growing vegetables, and

by using the land in other ways. But we know that what is actually happening is that many of these veterans who have three acres of land are not using it at all. Their land has become a liability on them. They find it difficult to keep it cultivated and stop the weeds from growing, so they will not run foul of the town inspectors, who do not like to see unsightly pieces of land in their vicinity.
I know that out west many of the officials feel it would be a good thing if the provision for three acres were reduced to half an acre. The minister may reply that if that were done it would be made into a housing project. Well, what would be wrong with that? If veterans need homes, and if we can help them to get homes by reducing the requirement to half an acre instead of three acres, I think consideration should be given to this.
There is one other matter I should like to mention in connection with the Pension Act. I would like to see the committee on veterans affairs set up with broad terms of reference so they could review some of the amendments made a few years ago. At one time we made an amendment to section 11 (c) of the act by striking out certain words, because we felt that by so doing we would make the pension available to veterans who had been refused pensions on the ground that their disabilities were of pre-enlistment origin. I should like to know what effect that amendment has had, how many veterans' applications have been reviewed, and how many of those applications have now been granted as a result of that amendment.
Then I would like to see a review of the results of the amendment we made to section 63. That section deals with the benefit of the doubt. We amended the section in order to assure that the veteran did in reality get the full benefit of the doubt. That is another matter I should like to see investigated in order that we may find out whether it is doing the thing we intended it should do. If those two amendments have not accomplished what the committee wanted them to accomplish then I think it is up to the government to provide additional amendments to the legislation in order to assure that every veteran who is really entitled to pension gets the full benefit of the doubt.
In conclusion I again urge the government to give careful consideration to making the veterans' committee a standing committee in order that the various grievances of the veterans may be considered from time to time.

Mr. Chairman, I want to express my disappointment that nothing has been done this session to improve the position of recipients of war veterans allowance. I think that disappointment is shared by all the veterans in Canada. It was hoped that this year there would be some increase in the rate of war veterans allowance. I do not intend to repeat the arguments which have been made by several hon. members who have said that an increase not only is justified but is absolutely essential at this time. I think the increased cost of living is sufficient in itself to show why an increase is required in the rate.
In addition to increasing the rate I should like to see some action taken to raise the ceiling on allowable earnings by recipients of war veterans allowance. I have never been able to understand why a war veterans allowance recipient was limited to the small amount of allowable earnings which has been the case up to date. It would seem to me only reasonable that he should be permitted to have an income up to the minimum at which income tax is imposed. The fact that he is limited to the extent he is causes great difficulty to these recipients of war veterans allowances.
I would say that the majority of the cases with which I have come in personal contact during the past two or three years have been due to the fact that over a certain period of time these recipients of war veterans allowance have made a certain amount of money. Generally the amount was not very much, but the man might not report it or forget to report it or something like that. Eventually it would be discovered that he had made this money and his war veterans allowance would be cut off, or a certain amount would be deducted from his monthly cheque. The result was that in many cases the war veteran would be left in a desperate situation, where it was practically impossible for him to live.
All that suffering, all those difficulties could be overcome by lifting the ceiling. There would be no cost to the public treasury in doing that. It is not as if this would necessitate paying out more money. The lifting of the ceiling would not cost the taxpayer any more money, but it certainly would make things much more pleasant for the recipients of war veterans allowance. They should be allowed sufficient to permit a bare living standard, which is not possible at the present time for many of them.
